passage:
On the first Monday of each month, Tushar's team at the Pune office held what they called 'bad news tea'. Anyone could bring a problem, a missed deadline or a shortcut someone was tempted by, and whoever flagged the most useful one got first pick of the samosas and a mention in the company newsletter.
Today Ganga raised her hand. 'The new partner wants us to skip two identity checks to sign up clients faster.'
Tushar didn't flinch. 'Thank you. That's a line we've already agreed we won't cross. I'll take it to the review committee.'
Later he opened the note pinned on his laptop screen: three lines he had written when he became team lead. The second read: If I catch myself explaining away a bad feeling, stop and ask someone.
He added today's date beside it.

qa.q: What did the new partner want the team to skip?
qa.a: The partner wanted them to skip two identity checks to sign up clients faster.

qa.q: Why doesn't Tushar flinch at Ganga's news?
qa.a: He decided his lines in advance and trusts the process, so bad news feels like something to handle rather than hide.

qa.q: What in this team's habits guards against drift?
qa.a: Regular 'bad news tea' rewards people for raising problems, a review committee takes them up, and Tushar keeps pre-written lines to check himself against.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel raising the problem in this team?
qa.a: Ganga likely feels safe and even valued, knowing a warning will be thanked and acted on rather than punished.

grounding: It shows a team rewarding honest bad news through a regular forum and a leader who set his lines in advance and watches for explaining away discomfort.

passage:
'So what exactly changes?' Keerthana asked, stirring coffee in the office canteen.
'Three things,' Ayesha said. 'An anonymous line that goes to the board, not to managers. Bonuses tied to audit results as well as sales. And every quarter, a prize for whoever raises the most useful bad news.'
'A prize for bad news? The old bosses would have fainted.'
'The old bosses are why we had the recall.'
Keerthana was quiet for a moment. 'I knew about the labels, you know. Back then. I told myself it wasn't my department.'
'Most of us told ourselves something.'
'So how do I stop doing that?'
Ayesha pulled a card from a wallet. 'I wrote my lines down the week I joined. Things I won't sign, whatever the target. When I start explaining something away, I read this.'
Keerthana took a photo of it.

qa.q: Where does the new anonymous line go?
qa.a: It goes to the board, not to managers.

qa.q: What does Keerthana's admission about the labels reveal?
qa.a: It reveals lingering guilt about staying silent before, and a wish not to explain away discomfort again.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do the next time a shortcut is suggested?
qa.a: Keerthana could write down personal lines in advance, like Ayesha's card, check them before signing anything, and use the anonymous line to the board if something still feels wrong.

qa.q: Why might Ayesha answer 'Most of us told ourselves something' instead of judging Keerthana?
qa.a: Ayesha seems to know how the old culture pushed many people to look away, so sharing the blame makes it easier for Keerthana to change instead of feeling ashamed.

grounding: It shows an organisation adding a safe reporting line, reviewing incentives and rewarding bad news, and a person keeping written lines to catch rationalising.
